newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing eyes services in globalisation drive.
newsitem.headline: Boeing eyes services in globalisation drive.

text.p: U.S. aircraft giant Boeing may expand into aerospace services as part of a long-term drive to become a global company and is on the lookout for foreign partners, chairman and chief executive officer Phil Condit said on Friday.

Seattle-based Boeing Co already has big ambitions and is awaiting regulatory approval from the U.S. and European authorities for a merger with McDonnell Douglas (MDD), which would create a firm with annual sales of $48 billion and 200,000 employees.

"I do have goals to increase Boeing's presence on a global basis... so that we are more active in a lot of countries," Condit told reporters here. "One of the areas that is very interesting is the broader...service area."
Boeing's core activities would however remain civil aircraft, defence and space, and any new business will build on its knowledge of its aerospace customers, he said.
Condit cited as an example its airline training joint venture with FlightSafety International, announced on March 10.

"That joint venture will have operations in a number of countries...It also gives us a presence and a place to understand (customers') needs more directly," he said. "I think it is possible to continue those kind of things, looking at other service opportunities."

Boeing will look for a pre-tax return on investment of of between 13 to 20 percent on new business, he said. The company was still examining the possibilities and did not yet have estimates of revenue or profit contributions.
Condit said he met European Competitin Commissioner Karel van Miert in Brussels earlier this week and reiterated that he expects approval of the MDD merger.

"I don't see any restrictions at this point," he said. "The overlap of the businesses is very little, so we're not faced with significant plant closures, we don't have products that overlap." he added, "There will be a lot of discussion, a lot of data, but in the end it will be approved."
The "strictly informational" meeting dealt with Boeing's strategy behind the merger decision and the Commission's review procedure. "We did not go into details," he said.
Condit played down anti-competitive fears expressed by European rival Airbus Industrie, especially in helicopters, saying they were in different markets.

Boeing makes twin-rotor, heavy lift helicopters, while McDonnell Douglas makes light, commercial products, he said. And with four U.S. helicopter makers, industry obervers have said there was room for consolidation, he added.
He denied it was in Boeing's interests to force its U.S. suppliers to stay away from partnering Airbus on its A3XX large plane project, as alleged by Airbus partner Daimler-Benz Aerospace.

Boeing wants its subcontractors to "have a broader business base, to spread overhead costs and deliver more economical products," he said. It also wants to expand collaboration with foreign companies, such as British Aerospace Plc (BAe).
There were no conflicts for BAe, which is an Airbus partner, in working with Boeing, he said.

A Boeing Australian unit supplies Airbus doors and parts, he said. Boeing is a supplier to BAe on the 1.9 billion pound Nimrod 2000 maritime patrol aircraft, and there was potential for BAe to work on the U.S. Joint Strike Fighter in which Boeing leads one of the two groups bidding for production rights.

Boeing's stock split, announced in February, was to attract individual investors, particularly its own employees, Condit said. "At prices of the middle $50 per share, the stock is more accessible to individual owners."
Boeing expects the MDD merger to generate around $1 billion of savings, mainly by cutting head office staff.

The biggest task in the merger will be to get 200,000 people working togther efficiently. He aimed to "break down barriers between organisations", adding that people will always put up new barriers whether they were organised around projects or processes. Breaking down boundaries "never stops," he said.
